articles.title: Pope Leo leads Sunday prayers in first major public appearance since lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV has made his first major public appearance since his lung cancer surgery, appearing at the same spot in the Vatican that he announced he was going in for an operation.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV has made his first major public appearance since his lung cancer surgery, saying the experience brought him closer to all those who suffer, from the same spot in the Vatican he announced a week ago he needed an operation. The 71-year-old pontiff lead the Sunday Angelus from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter’s Square, where thousands gathered to clap, sing and hear his message. Leo thanked doctors for his treatment and for all those who prayed for him, adding that he is gradually returning to his duties as pope. “This experience has given me a profound sense of closeness to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity,” he told crowds. “Now that this delicate phase has passed, I will gradually resume my activities – always with the help of God and your prayers. Thank you once again,” he added. The pope’s remarks came as thousands of runners taking part in the Rome marathon had been jogging up the main walkway leading into St. Peter’s Square taking a right past the papal residence of the Apostolic palace. At midday, however, all eyes were on Leo XIV when he appeared at the window of his home to address the crowd, wishing them a happy Sunday in a firm and strong voice. The pope was released on Saturday from the Gemelli hospital following lung surgery to remove a growth which was later diagnosed as an adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Doctors say he has made a good recovery following his surgery, even saying he can make trip to Latin America due to take place 6-17 November. “I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” Professor Stefano Margaritora, who operated on the pontiff, told Vatican news. Last Sunday the pope made his surprise announcement that a “nodule” had been found on his lung, and he was going to have surgery. The news of the cancer diagnosis on Tuesday shocked people inside the Vatican and across the Catholic world, given the pope was known for being in good physical shape. The pope’s visit to Latin America includes Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Leo served as a missionary and bishop in Peru for a number of years. His itinerary includes a stop in Cusco, which is around 3,350 meters above sea level, where there is roughly one-third less oxygen available per breath compared to sea-level. Sharon Braithwaite and Barbie Latza Nadeau contributed reporting.

articles.title: In 2024, an Iowa court let a farmer keep the family land his father had transferred to him, despite his siblings’ challenge
articles.summary: In a significant ruling, the Iowa Court of Appeals affirmed a farmer's ownership of family land in the Natvig v. Natvig case, amidst challenges from siblings alleging undue influence and estate planning disputes. The decision underscores the complexities of family farm succession and the importance of proper estate documentation.
articles.body: Family farms can represent more than a source of income. For some families, they carry a history of work, memories and dedication to keeping the land together. Yet succession, meaning who should inherit the land, can cause conflict if one child has worked the land while others want their share of the estate. In 2024, the Iowa Court of Appeals decided Natvig v. Natvig, a dispute over a family farm. In its opinion No. 23-1992, filed on 30 October 2024, the court affirmed the dismissal of a challenge to Michael Natvig’s ownership of farmland that his father, Godfrey Natvig, had transferred to him, holding that Michael had rebutted the presumption of undue influence. Michael’s siblings and two children of a late sibling had argued that the transfer was the product of undue influence and that the estate planning should be set aside.Godfrey Natvig’s transfers of 160 acres to MichaelGodfrey and his wife, Theodora, had eight children. Farming was very important to Godfrey and Michael lived and worked on the farm with his father for many years. In 1994, Godfrey and Theodora conveyed 40 acres to Michael. After Theodora died in 2002, Godfrey conveyed another 40 acres to Michael while keeping a life estate, which let him keep the right to use the land during his lifetime. In early 2016, Godfrey conveyed the remaining 80 acres to Michael by warranty deed, bringing the total transferred to Michael to 160 acres.Godfrey’s will, made in 2004, divided his estate equally among his eight children but gave Michael an option to buy the remaining 80 acres of farmland if the other heirs wanted to sell. In a codicil dated 20 May 2016, Godfrey wrote that he wanted the real estate to stay in the family. The codicil said the last 80-acre tract had been conveyed to Michael in return for services he had rendered, was rendering and would render in the future, and it left all real estate to Michael. These details come from the Iowa Court of Appeals’ opinion.Siblings challenged the transfer and estate plansGodfrey’s other children and two of his grandchildren challenged the arrangements. They alleged fraud, undue influence and duress and claimed that an insane delusion shaped Godfrey’s estate planning. They argued that Godfrey wrongly believed his children planned to sell the 80 acres after his death. They also challenged Michael’s actions as their father’s attorney-in-fact, a role that let him make certain decisions for Godfrey, including what they described as gifts Michael made to himself. Both courts accepted Michael’s explanation that the money went to Godfrey’s care and expenses or was spent at Godfrey’s direction.In early 2017, the siblings asked a court to remove Michael as Godfrey’s attorney-in-fact, alleging breach of fiduciary duty. Godfrey intervened and testified and the district court found that he had the capacity to revoke Michael’s power of attorney if he chose to. It dismissed the petition. Godfrey died in 2018 and Michael became executor of his estate. In 2019, the siblings filed a new action alleging that the 2016 codicil was procured by undue influence and that Michael obtained the 80-acre deed while acting as Godfrey’s attorney-in-fact. At a three-day trial, the district court heard from Michael, six of his siblings, Godfrey’s attorney, physician, tax preparer and caregiver and other witnesses. The court dismissed the siblings’ petition and they appealed.Independent legal advice supported the transferThe question was whether Michael had improperly influenced his father or whether Godfrey had voluntarily chosen to transfer the land. Because Michael and Godfrey were in a confidential relationship, which Michael did not dispute, Iowa law presumed the transfer was the product of undue influence. Michael therefore had to rebut the presumption with clear, convincing and satisfactory evidence that he acted in good faith and that Godfrey gave the land freely, intelligently and voluntarily. Iowa law treats proper independent advice as one way to show a grantor acted freely, so the court weighed evidence that Godfrey had the benefit of such advice before the transfer. Godfrey’s physician had also evaluated Godfrey’s ability to manage legal transactions. In January 2016, Dr. Paul Jensen concluded that Godfrey was capable of understanding the ramifications of the decisions and changes he might need to make.Godfrey’s lawyer, Erik Fern, testified about their discussion of why Godfrey wanted Michael to have the land. The court also rejected the insane-delusion argument. The siblings disputed Godfrey’s belief about what his children intended to do with the land, but the court found that the belief did not amount to an insane delusion, which Iowa law defines as a belief with no basis in reason that cannot be dispelled by argument.The Iowa Court of Appeals affirmed on 30 October 2024The court of appeals affirmed the district court’s dismissal, leaving the farmland transfer and Godfrey’s estate plan intact. It noted that the final 80 acres were part of a pattern of earlier transfers to Michael and that opportunity alone was not enough to support an inference of undue influence. The decision did not mean that a parent can always leave a family farm to one child without challenge. The ruling rested on the facts presented in this case. The full opinion is available on the Iowa Judicial Branch website.The case highlights the importance of documenting estate decisionsThe Natvig case illustrates the problems that can arise when a family farm passes from one generation to the next. A parent may see a transfer to the child who works the farm as recognition of years of hard work and care, as well as a way to preserve the property. Other children may see the same move as an unfair distribution of family assets. Independent legal advice, a clear record of the owner’s intentions and evidence that the decision was voluntary can play a significant role in such cases. The court looked at the circumstances of the transfer and did not treat the unequal result as misconduct in itself. For Godfrey Natvig, preserving the farm was the main concern and the Court of Appeal left the transfer standing as he had chosen.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: European Parliament votes to confront Muslim Brotherhood, 'Islamist entryism' in overwhelming vote
articles.summary: The European Parliament voted 'historic' 381-167 to condemn Islamist entryism and Muslim Brotherhood influence as critics say the hard part will be converting the resolution into legislation.
articles.body: Following the sanctioning of foreign Muslim Brotherhood groups by the Trump administration, the European Parliament recently took its own action against the transnational radical Islamist group. As Europe begins to respond to the threat of radical Islam across the continent, an overwhelming majority of the European Parliament voted for a resolution that condemned the Muslim Brotherhood and its actions. European Parliament member Céline Imart of France, who sponsored the resolution, called the vote "a historic victory because it is a European first. For the first time, Europe has voted on a text that tackles Islamist entryism and the Muslim Brotherhood." EUROPE’S LEFT COURTS MUSLIM VOTERS AS ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICS RESHAPE CONTINENT Imart posted on X that she had "broken a taboo that Europe has been dragging around like a chain: this victory signifies a major doctrinal shift in the institutions… We were able to transcend partisan divides on a major issue for our societies and our youth." Lorenzo Vidino, director of the program on extremism at George Washington University, told Fox News Digital that, "This is something that the French and the Austrian governments have been pushing for almost a decade," noting a growing consensus across Europe that wants action. The resolution was led by the European People’s Party, or EPP, a center-right coalition that is the largest group in the European Parliament. "The voting does reflect a gap between the right and the left," said Vidino, "with the right voting almost entirely in favor of the resolution, and a good part of the left, although with some notable exceptions, voting against it." As part of her post on X, Imart made it a point to thank "the negotiators from the other groups with whom I had the pleasure of working - excluding the socialists and the far left, who boycotted the text." Vidino said, "The Brotherhood remains something that is seen through the political lenses of our own political debates, where it shouldn't be... because it's a challenge to our societies." DENMARK'S LEFT-WING PM WARNS: 'BIG ENEMY HAS STARTED TO GROW FROM WITHIN' AS EUROPE FACES MIGRANT RECKONING A press release on the resolution issued by the European Parliament's news website stated that Islamist entryism targets "democratic institutions, the rule of law, equality between women and men and fundamental freedoms." It stressed that Muslim citizens must be protected from discrimination as "a democratic obligation," while "warning against treating organized Islamist networks as representative interlocutors." The release also stated, "While Europe must remain free, open and faithful to its principles, it can ‘no longer fund, consult or legitimize networks that use its language, procedures and funding to weaken its values from within,’" but "MEPs stress that anti-discrimination policies must not be used to shield Islam from criticism or legitimize organized Islamist networks." The resolution was slammed by ENAR, a pan-European anti-racism network, which released a statement following its passage. "ENAR condemns in the strongest possible terms the racist and Islamophobic resolution "on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network" proposed by the European People’s Party (EPP) and passed by the European Parliament today, including its targeting of ENAR and its members like FEMYSO through sham allegations and falsehoods seeking to associate our network with the Muslim Brotherhood. ENAR categorically rejects these claims." It added in part, "This resolution is a stain on the European Parliament and marks a profoundly shameful day in Europe’s history. A Parliament that should defend democracy, equality and fundamental rights has instead given institutional legitimacy to a racist politics of suspicion that casts Muslim communities, Muslim-led civil society, organizations combating Islamophobia, and those who defend their rights as inherently suspect." Edmund Fitton-Brown, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital "This resolution is where the pushback begins against Islamist entryism in Europe. It is admirably clearly worded. The task of converting it into binding legislation begins now and will be difficult." The former UK ambassador to Yemen, Fitton-Brown added, "Europe regularly imagines that "legal", "non-violent" Islamism is in conflict with, and a potential antidote to, violent Islamist terrorism. It is not, it is a gateway to it, it creates the climate for it, and the two are pursuing the same goals, only via different tactics." He added, "Europe fails to prioritize subversion as a threat, whereas during the Cold War it understood that threat and took serious measures to counter it. Europe also seeks to appease Islamist entryism by adopting hostile policies towards Israel, and sometimes by passing blasphemy-adjacent and anti-"Islamophobia" laws, thinking they are protecting the Muslim community. In fact, the main victims of these laws are liberal Muslims trying to escape the confines of their community and enjoy Western freedoms." Asked about the differences between Europe and the U.S. approach to the Brotherhood, Vidino said the European way is "a bit more nuanced" than that of the U.S., where the Trump administration has designated the Muslim Brotherhood and 4 of its branches as terrorist organizations. He says Europe sees the Muslim Brotherhood "mostly through the lenses of entryism, of subversion, of a group that destroys the fabrics of society… a matter of a threat to democracy, but a lot of the activities of the Brotherhood might be legal if taken individually." TRUMP ADMIN ACCUSES HAMAS OF BACKING GAZA FLOTILLA, SANCTIONS ACTIVIST AND MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD NETWORKS While noting that numerous security services across Europe have been warning about the Muslim Brotherhood for some time, Vidino says the resolution "sets the tone. It gives a political push," suggesting agencies and governments "might feel more legitimized in seeing the Brotherhood in negative ways." "I'm a bit skeptical on whether this resolution would have a major tangible impact," Vidino added. "Islamist groups are very good at camouflaging their activities." While there is "no organization that calls itself Muslim Brotherhood in Europe," he said if and when funding is pulled from an Islamist organization by the EU, "They will make a fuss… They fight back. They have an ability to also leverage what could be a crisis, but turn it to their advantage by playing the victim card and the Islamophobia card." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As part of the resolution, the European Council was asked to assess whether entities or individuals linked to the Muslim Brotherhood should be added to the EU list of terrorist organizations. It called for full traceability of EU funding and a European Commission overview of EU funds awarded to people or entities suspected of links to the Muslim Brotherhood or political Islam. It also welcomed initiatives by member states to draw up national lists of hate preachers and calls for the establishment of such a list at EU level, while also calling for stronger scrutiny of foreign funding and transnational partnerships, particularly involving actors linked to Qatar or Turkey and greater use of Schengen tools and EU databases. "This vote is a victory, but it is also a starting point," Imart said. "The Commission and the Council must now take action, and I will make sure they do."
